claim: GCNA1 and TRA98 antibodies recognize the same previously unannotated protein in mouse.
source: Mass spectrometry indicates that GCNA1 and TRA98 antibodies immunoprecipitate the same protein.
evidence: Mass spectrometry data showing peptide coverage of the same protein from both antibody immunoprecipitations, and Western blot showing depletion of both antigens in mutant ES cells.

claim: Mouse GCNA is predicted to be entirely disordered.
source: Based on its extreme negative charge and atypical amino acid composition, mouse GCNA is predicted to be entirely disordered (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2A).
evidence: Computational prediction using disorder prediction algorithms and charge-hydropathy analysis.

claim: Mouse GCNA has a theoretical isoelectric point of 4.17, making it more acidic than 98.9% of all mouse proteins.
source: Mouse GCNA contains four distinct repeat classes that comprise the majority of the protein, and its theoretical isoelectric point of 4.17 makes it more acidic than 98.9% of all mouse proteins (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Bjellqvist et al., 1993).
evidence: Calculated isoelectric point compared to distribution of all mouse proteins.

claim: GCNA forms a distinctive coating around condensed chromosomes in meiotic prophase.
source: GCNA coats condensed chromosomes during meiotic prophase. One plane through a single nucleus of a male spermatocyte in the zygotene phase of Meiosis I is shown.
evidence: Immunofluorescence imaging showing GCNA localization on chromosomes during meiosis.

claim: Human GCNA contains a protease domain, a C2C2 zinc finger, and an HMG box in addition to an IDR, while mouse GCNA lacks these structured domains.
source: Human GCNA shares a region with the same acidic and repetitive character (green) and contains additional, ordered domains – a protease domain (blue), and a C2C2 zinc finger (purple).
evidence: Domain architecture analysis and comparison between mouse and human GCNA proteins.

claim: The structured domains were lost more than 25 million years ago in the rodent lineage.
source: Specifically, we deduced that three domains had been lost more than 25 million years ago in the rodent lineage (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis and identification of non-transcribed pseudo-exons in mouse genome.

claim: Non-transcribed pseudo-exons that previously encoded structured domains are found in the mouse genome.
source: Non-transcribed pseudo-exons that previously encoded these domains are found in the mouse genome, allowing us to confidently place mouse GCNA into this larger family (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Genomic sequence analysis showing remnants of exons encoding structured domains.

claim: GCNA orthologs are present in every eukaryotic superkingdom.
source: GCNA orthologs are present in every eukaryotic superkingdom (Figure 4A) (Simpson and Roger, 2004).
evidence: Identification of GCNA orthologs across diverse eukaryotic species using HMM-based searches.

claim: GCNA proteins were present in the common ancestor of eukaryotes, more than 2 billion years ago.
source: Taken together, our analyses lead us to infer that GCNA proteins were present in the common ancestor of eukaryotes, more than 2 billion years ago.
evidence: Phylogenetic distribution of GCNA orthologs across all major eukaryotic lineages.

claim: A typical GCNA protein has four components: a large IDR, a zinc metalloprotease domain, a C2C2 zinc finger, and a non-canonical two-helix HMG box.
source: Our analyses of these orthologs allowed us to deduce that a typical GCNA protein has four components: a large IDR, a zinc metalloprotease domain, a C2C2 zinc finger, and a non-canonical two-helix HMG box (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Domain analysis across multiple GCNA orthologs and HMM construction.

claim: YABBY proteins are GCNA family members that have diverged in the 600 million years since the last common ancestor of algae and higher plants.
source: Based on our phylogenetic analyses of HMG boxes (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), we propose that YABBY proteins are GCNA family members that have diverged in the 600 million years since the last common ancestor of algae (where canonical four-domain GCNA proteins are still found) and higher plants.
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis of HMG boxes and domain composition comparison.

claim: In S. pombe, transcription of Gcna is 17-fold upregulated during meiosis relative to vegetative cells.
source: In S. pombe, transcription of Gcna is 17-fold upregulated during meiosis relative to vegetative cells (Mata et al., 2002).
evidence: Published transcriptome data from S. pombe.

claim: In Chlamydomonas, Gcna is upregulated 17-fold in activated gametes relative to vegetative cells.
source: Likewise, in Chlamydomonas, a single-celled green alga, Gcna is upregulated 17-fold in activated gametes relative to vegetative cells (Ning et al., 2013).
evidence: Published transcriptome data from Chlamydomonas.

claim: In Hydra, Gcna expression is upregulated in interstitial stem cells compared with two exclusively somatic stem cell lineages.
source: In the cnidarian Hydra, germ cells are derived from interstitial stem cells, where Gcna expression is upregulated compared with two exclusively somatic stem cell lineages (Littlefield, 1985; Bosch et al., 2010; Hemmrich et al., 2012).
evidence: Published expression data from Hydra stem cell populations.

claim: In planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea, Gcna is upregulated in neoblasts and enriched in testes.
source: In the planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea, and the acoel Hofstenia miamia, Gcna is upregulated in neoblasts, the totipotent adult stem cell populations from which germ cells arise (van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Srivastava et al., 2014). Transcripts of this gene are also enriched in the testes in a sexual strain of Schmidtea (Figure 5A).
evidence: Published expression data and in situ hybridization showing Gcna expression in neoblasts and testes.

claim: Mouse Gcna transcript shows a 13-fold upregulation in the testis compared to somatic tissues.
source: Likewise, mouse, which specifies germ cells later in the embryo through inductive signals, shows a 13-fold upregulation of Gcna transcript in the testis compared to somatic tissues (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: Expression data comparing testis to somatic tissues.

claim: Mouse GCNA protein is germ-cell specific despite transcript presence in somatic tissues.
source: Transcripts in somatic tissues are apparently not translated, as mouse GCNA protein is germ-cell specific (Maatouk et al., 2006).
evidence: Published protein localization data showing germ cell specificity.

claim: Human GCNA protein is localized to the nucleus of germ cells.
source: Like mouse GCNA protein, the human ortholog is localized to the nucleus of germ cells (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry showing nuclear localization in human germ cells.

claim: C. elegans gcna-1 mutants exhibit a significant reduction in brood size at 25 degrees Celsius.
source: Worms carrying either of the gcna-1 mutant alleles have small but significant reductions in brood size at 25 degrees Celsius (Figure 6A).
evidence: Brood size counts from two independent mutant alleles compared to wildtype.

claim: C. elegans gcna-1 mutants exhibit a significant HIM (High Incidence of Males) phenotype.
source: Additionally, both alleles exhibit a significant HIM phenotype, substantiating a reproductive function for GCNA in C. elegans (Figure 6B).
evidence: Male frequency counts from two independent mutant alleles showing increased male progeny.

claim: Mutating Gcna dramatically impairs male fertility in mice, with 10 of 11 Gcna-mutant males siring no offspring.
source: We found that mutating Gcna dramatically impairs male fertility, a testament to the importance of the IDR; 10 of 11 Gcna-mutant males tested sired no offspring, while wild-type male controls sired 5 to 24 offspring (Figure 7A).
evidence: Fertility testing data showing number of litters and pups from mutant and wildtype males.

claim: The epididymal duct in Gcna-mutant mice is nearly devoid of sperm.
source: The epididymal duct, which contains copious amounts of maturing sperm in wildtype mice, was nearly devoid of sperm in the mutant (Figure 7B).
evidence: Histological analysis of epididymal ducts comparing mutant and wildtype mice.

claim: Gcna-mutant female mice are fertile.
source: Gcna-mutant female mice were fertile (data not shown).
evidence: Fertility testing of female mutant mice.

claim: GCNA proteins are members of a small family of IDR-containing metalloproteases that includes Wss1 and Spartan.
source: Through phylogenetic analysis as well as structural modeling, we determined that GCNA proteins are members of a small family of IDR-containing metalloproteases that includes only two other members, Wss1 and Spartan, both of which have essential functions in DNA repair coupled to DNA replication (Mosbech et al., 2012; Centore et al., 2012; Davis et al., 2012; Juhasz et al., 2012; Machida et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2013; Stingele et al., 2014; Balakirev et al., 2015).
evidence: Phylogenetic analysis and structural modeling showing relationship to Wss1 and Spartan.

claim: GCNA, Wss1, and Spartan proteins share three common elements: minigluzincin protease domains, large intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), and motifs for binding ubiquitin family proteins (particularly SUMO interacting motifs, or SIMs).
source: GCNA, Wss1, and Spartan proteins share three common elements: minigluzincin protease domains, large intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), and motifs for binding ubiquitin family proteins (particularly SUMO interacting motifs, or SIMs).
evidence: Domain analysis and motif identification across the three protein families.

claim: Secondary structure prediction and 3D modeling place GCNA, Wss1, and Spartan within the minigluzincin protease family.
source: Secondary structure prediction and 3D modeling place all three proteins within the minigluzincin protease family (Figure 8B) (Balakirev et al., 2015; López-Pelegrín et al., 2013).
evidence: Structural modeling and comparison showing similarity to minigluzincin proteases.

claim: GCNA, Spartan, and Wss1 proteases are more closely related to each other than they are to any other protein family among more than 14,800 PfamA curated protein families.
source: We conducted HMM to HMM comparison across more than 14,800 PfamA curated protein families, including over 200 protease families, using alignment and secondary structure scoring. We found that GCNA, Spartan, and Wss1 proteases are more closely related to each other than they are to any other protein family (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: HMM-to-HMM comparison across comprehensive protein family database.

claim: Wss1 and Spartan protease domains and SUMO interacting motifs are essential for response to DNA damage caused by ionizing radiation, UV light, and chemical crosslinkers.
source: Wss1 and Spartan protease domains and SUMO interacting motifs are essential for response to DNA damage caused by ionizing radiation, UV light, and chemical crosslinkers (Centore et al., 2012; Stingele et al., 2014).
evidence: Published functional studies of Wss1 and Spartan in DNA damage response.

claim: GCNA may function in maintenance of genome integrity in cells whose genomes will be passed to the next generation.
source: By extrapolation, we propose that the GCNA protein family identified here may also function in maintenance of genome integrity, and has become specialized for cells whose genomes will be passed to the next generation.
evidence: Inference based on homology to Wss1 and Spartan proteins with known DNA repair functions.

claim: The phenotype of Gcna mutant mice is similar to those of other genes involved in DNA damage repair, including Rad18 and Rad6.
source: The phenotype of Gcna mutant mice is similar to those of other genes involved in DNA damage repair, including Rad18 and Rad6, which function in the same DNA damage tolerance pathway as Spartan (Inagaki, 2011; Roest et al., 1996; Hedglin and Benkovic, 2015).
evidence: Comparison of mutant phenotypes with published data on DNA repair gene mutants.

claim: The HIM phenotype in Gcna-deficient C. elegans is consistent with a defect in genome maintenance.
source: Likewise, the HIM phenotype in Gcna-deficient C. elegans is consistent with a defect in genome maintenance (Billi et al., 2014); in C. elegans as well as mammals, efficient and proper repair of meiotic double strand breaks is crucial for accurate chromosome segregation (Baudat et al., 2013; Youds and Boulton, 2011).
evidence: Interpretation of HIM phenotype in context of known genome maintenance mechanisms.

claim: GCNA arose prior to the divergence of the major eukaryotic lineages and predates the origin of a dedicated germline by a billion years.
source: Unlike most of these genes (Eirín-López and Ausió, 2011; Kerner et al., 2011), GCNA arose prior to the divergence of the major eukaryotic lineages. GCNA is more ancient than all but Piwi and associated proteins that function in small-RNA-mediated genome defense (Kerner et al., 2011; Swarts et al., 2014), and predates the origin of a dedicated metazoan germline by a billion years.
evidence: Phylogenetic distribution and timing analysis compared to other germline genes.

claim: GCNA has functioned in reproduction for at least 600 million years.
source: Studies of Gcna-mutant C. elegans and mice indicate that GCNA has functioned in reproduction for at least 600 million years.
evidence: Functional studies in two organisms whose last common ancestor lived 600 million years ago.

claim: Gcna gene expression is enriched in reproductive cells across eukarya – either just prior to or during meiosis in single-celled eukaryotes, and in stem cells and germ cells of diverse multicellular animals.
source: Gcna gene expression is enriched in reproductive cells across eukarya – either just prior to or during meiosis in single-celled eukaryotes, and in stem cells and germ cells of diverse multicellular animals.
evidence: Expression data from multiple species across eukaryotic diversity.

claim: GCNA proteins may protect the genomic integrity of cells carrying a heritable genome.
source: Homology to IDR-containing proteins implicated in DNA damage repair suggests that GCNA proteins may protect the genomic integrity of cells carrying a heritable genome.
evidence: Inference based on homology to DNA repair proteins and expression pattern in reproductive cells.

claim: Meiosis is believed to have evolved once, in the common ancestor of extant eukaryotes, about two billion years ago.
source: Meiosis is believed to have evolved once, in the common ancestor of extant eukaryotes, about two billion years ago (Ramesh et al., 2005; Villeneuve and Hillers, 2001).
evidence: Published evolutionary analyses of meiosis.

claim: An RNAi pathway that likely functioned in defense against transposons and viruses evolved in early eukaryotes.
source: At the same time, special protection for heritable genomes evolved in the form of an RNAi pathway that likely functioned in defense against transposons and viruses (Cerutti and Casas-Mollano, 2006; Shabalina and Koonin, 2008).
evidence: Published evolutionary analyses of RNAi pathways.

claim: GCNA is expressed concomitant with entry into the genital ridge along with classical germ cell factors DAZL and DDX4 (MVH).
source: The handful of proteins that are expressed concomitant with entry into the genital ridge include the classical germ cell factors DAZL and DDX4 (Mouse Vasa Homolog; MVH) and the antigens recognized by GCNA1 and TRA98 antibodies (Figure 1A) (Hu et al., 2015; Enders and May, 1994; Tanaka et al., 2000).
evidence: Published expression data and immunofluorescence showing co-expression with known germ cell markers.

claim: GCNA1 and TRA98 monoclonal antibodies show no reactivity to somatic cells.
source: The GCNA1 and TRA98 monoclonal antibodies, generated independently from rats immunized with cell lysates from adult mouse testis, are robust markers of mouse germ cell nuclei and show no reactivity to somatic cells (Enders and May, 1994; Tanaka et al., 2000).
evidence: Published characterization of antibody specificity.

claim: Both GCNA1 and TRA98 antibodies recognize a fragment containing a murine-specific 8-amino-acid tandem GE(P/M/S)E(S/T)EAK repeat that occurs 25 times in the protein.
source: By expressing portions of mouse GCNA in bacteria, we determined that both antibodies recognize a fragment containing a murine-specific 8-amino-acid tandem GE(P/M/S)E(S/T)EAK repeat that occurs 25 times in the protein (Figure 1D,E).
evidence: Bacterial expression and Western blot analysis mapping antibody epitopes.

claim: IDRs display conformational flexibility and have no single, well-defined equilibrium structure.
source: IDRs display conformational flexibility and have no single, well-defined equilibrium structure, and yet carry out numerous biological activities (van der Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Published review of intrinsically disordered protein properties.

claim: IDRs have high absolute net charge due to enrichment for disorder-promoting (charged and polar) amino acids, and low net hydrophobicity due to depletion of hydrophobic and order-promoting amino acids.
source: IDRs have high absolute net charge due to enrichment for disorder-promoting (charged and polar) amino acids, and low net hydrophobicity due to depletion of hydrophobic and order-promoting amino acids, features that make it possible to predict disordered regions from primary amino acid sequence alone (Uversky et al., 2000; He et al., 2009).
evidence: Published methods for predicting protein disorder from sequence.

claim: The overall amino acid composition of IDRs is often conserved in orthologous disordered protein families.
source: Despite a lack of primary sequence conservation, the overall amino acid composition of IDRs is often conserved in orthologous disordered protein families, as it is not the exact sequence of amino acids, but the overall character of the IDR – such as an abundance of residues that may be post-translationally modified, net charge, and amino acid enrichments and depletions – that confers function (van der Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Published analysis of IDR conservation patterns.

claim: GCNA IDRs have characteristic amino acid enrichments and depletions – some shared with proteins in a disordered dataset (DisProt) and others specific to the GCNA family.
source: A survey of the IDR composition of over 100 GCNA proteins across eukarya revealed that GCNA IDRs have characteristic amino acid enrichments and depletions – some shared with proteins in a disordered dataset (DisProt) and others specific to the GCNA family (Figure 2C).
evidence: Amino acid composition analysis comparing GCNA IDRs to known disordered and ordered protein datasets.

claim: GCNA proteins across species share short, linear protein-protein interaction motifs embedded within a larger disordered context.
source: In keeping with another common IDR paradigm, GCNA proteins across species, including mouse and human, share short, linear protein-protein interaction motifs embedded within a larger disordered context (Figure 1D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2) (van der Lee et al., 2014; Davey et al., 2015).
evidence: Motif analysis showing conserved short linear motifs (SIMs) across GCNA orthologs.

claim: Greater than 30% of proteins have disordered segments of 30 or more consecutive residues.
source: Protein disorder is ubiquitously present in eukaryotic proteomes; greater than 30% of proteins have disordered segments of 30 or more consecutive residues (Dunker et al., 2000).
evidence: Published proteome-wide analysis of protein disorder.

claim: IDRs dynamically interconvert between an ensemble of conformations separated by low energy barriers.
source: IDRs, rather than having a single, well-defined fold, dynamically interconvert between an ensemble of conformations separated by low energy barriers (Chebaro et al., 2015).
evidence: Published biophysical characterization of IDR dynamics.

claim: IDRs have critical biological functions across a wide variety of cellular processes including transcription, regulatory, and signaling pathways.
source: IDRs have critical biological functions across a wide variety of cellular processes including transcription, regulatory, and signaling pathways, and it has been proposed that IDRs support the processes that underlie the development of multicellular organisms (Xie et al., 2007; Tantos et al., 2012; Dunker et al., 2015).
evidence: Published reviews of IDR functions in cellular processes.

claim: Male sterility caused by mutation of the entirely disordered mouse GCNA indicates that the function of GCNA proteins lies at least in part in the disordered region.
source: Male sterility caused by mutation of the entirely disordered mouse GCNA indicates that the function of GCNA proteins lies at least in part in the disordered region.
evidence: Functional data from mouse mutants lacking only the IDR (no structured domains present).

claim: GCNA IDRs may function in molecular recognition mediated by SUMO interacting motifs, thereby recruiting or scaffolding larger protein complexes.
source: Homology with Wss1 and Spartan proteins suggests that GCNA IDRs function in molecular recognition mediated by SUMO interacting motifs, thereby recruiting or scaffolding larger protein complexes.
evidence: Inference based on homology to Wss1 and Spartan and presence of SIMs.

claim: GCNA IDRs may contribute to nucleic acid binding, either alone or in combination with the zinc finger and HMG box.
source: GCNA IDRs may also contribute to nucleic acid binding, either alone or in combination with the zinc finger and HMG box.
evidence: Speculation based on presence of nucleic acid binding domains and IDR properties.

claim: Sex chromosomes are enriched for genes encoding germ cell genes and are also enriched for disordered proteins.
source: GCNA may be among the first of many disordered protein families to be implicated in reproduction, as sex chromosomes, which have been shown to be enriched for genes encoding germ cell genes, are also enriched for disordered proteins (Mueller et al., 2013; Hegyi and Tompa, 2012).
evidence: Published analyses of sex chromosome gene content and protein disorder.

claim: Spermatogenesis and meiosis are among the biological processes most strongly correlated with predicted protein disorder.
source: Spermatogenesis and meiosis are in fact among the biological processes most strongly correlated with predicted protein disorder (Dunker et al., 2015).
evidence: Published analysis of protein disorder enrichment in biological processes.

claim: Conservation of structured domains in the GCNA family over a vast evolutionary timescale suggests that significant function likely also derives from these domains.
source: Conservation of structured domains in the GCNA family over a vast evolutionary timescale suggests that significant function likely also derives from these domains.
evidence: Inference based on evolutionary conservation of domains across billions of years.

claim: GCNA may help cells cope with the additional DNA damage burden that accompanies meiosis, a process that involves extensive, programmed DNA damage.
source: As such, GCNA may help cells cope with the additional DNA damage burden that accompanies meiosis, a process that involves extensive, programmed DNA damage (Keeney, 2008).
evidence: Speculation based on homology to DNA repair proteins and expression during meiosis.

claim: Sex-specific infertility is a common phenomenon in mice and is thought to be due to different levels of checkpoint control in males and females.
source: Sex-specific infertility is a common phenomenon in mice, and is thought to be due to different levels of checkpoint control in males and females (Matzuk and Lamb, 2002; Morelli and Cohen, 2005; Hunt and Hassold, 2002).
evidence: Published reviews of sex-specific fertility phenotypes in mice.

claim: GCNA joins a cohort of genes known for their function in metazoan germ cells, including Dazl/Boule, Vasa, Nanos, and Piwi.
source: GCNA joins a well studied cohort of genes, including Dazl/Boule, Vasa, Nanos, and Piwi, known for their function in metazoan germ cells.
evidence: Comparison to known germline genes.

claim: Many germline genes are proposed to be part of a conserved germline multipotency program (GMP) that functions in multipotent cells as well as in the germline.
source: Many of these genes are proposed to be part of a conserved germline multipotency program (GMP) that functions in multipotent cells as well as in the germline, where they have a broad role in establishing and maintaining pluripotency (Ewen-Campen et al., 2010; Juliano et al., 2010).
evidence: Published hypothesis about germline multipotency program.

claim: GCNA's role may be more fundamental than the ancestral pluripotency module and the GMP that arose from it.
source: We believe that GCNA's presence in the last common ancestor of extant eukaryotes indicates that GCNA's role is more fundamental than even the ancestral pluripotency module and the GMP that arose from it.
evidence: Inference based on GCNA's ancient origin predating the GMP.

claim: Like Piwi, GCNA proteins may perform a role that is critical for reproductive cells by helping to maintain the integrity and stability of heritable genomes across the generations.
source: Like Piwi, GCNA proteins may perform a role that is critical for reproductive cells by helping to maintain the integrity and stability of heritable genomes across the generations.
evidence: Speculation based on ancient origin, expression pattern, and homology to DNA repair proteins.

claim: The identity of GCNA1 and TRA98 antigens has remained unknown across 22 years of research and >425 publications in mouse reproductive biology.
source: Across 22 years of research, and >425 publications in mouse reproductive biology, investigators have employed antibodies to two antigens – GCNA1 and TRA98 – to distinguish germ cells from somatic cells. Nonetheless, the identity of the antigens themselves has remained unknown.
evidence: Historical context of antibody use without antigen identification.

claim: C. elegans gcna-1 encodes a canonical GCNA protein with an IDR, protease domain, zinc finger, and HMG box.
source: C. elegans gcna-1 encodes a canonical GCNA protein with an IDR, protease domain, zinc finger, and HMG box.
evidence: Domain analysis of C. elegans GCNA protein.

claim: The large IDR is retained in GCNA proteins almost without exception even when other domains are lost over evolutionary time.
source: Even in the face of other domains being lost over evolutionary time, the large IDR is retained in GCNA proteins almost without exception.
evidence: Comparative analysis of domain architecture across GCNA orthologs.

claim: C. elegans gcna-1 was reported to have a low penetrance HIM phenotype in an RNAi screen.
source: C. elegans gcna-1 had been depleted as part of an RNAi screen of germline-enriched genes (Colaiácovo et al., 2002). gcna-1 was reported to have a low penetrance HIM (High Incidence of Males) phenotype, suggestive of a defect in meiotic chromosome segregation, as XO male progeny result from nondisjunction in XX hermaphrodites.
evidence: Published RNAi screen results.

claim: Rapid evolution often renders IDRs un-alignable even among closely related species.
source: Because rapid evolution often renders IDRs un-alignable even among closely related species (Brown et al., 2010), primary sequence cannot be used to establish orthology.
evidence: Published analysis of IDR evolution and alignability.

claim: Mouse GCNA is encoded by a gene on the X chromosome.
source: Therefore, starting with mouse GCNA, which is encoded by a gene on the X chromosome, we identified orthologs in human and other vertebrates by synteny (Figure 3).
evidence: Genomic location data for mouse Gcna gene.

claim: Each species contains one Gcna gene, with certain exceptions including plants and protostomes such as drosophilids.
source: With certain exceptions including plants and protostomes such as drosophilids, each species contains one Gcna gene.
evidence: Survey of GCNA gene copy number across species.

claim: The four-domain architecture of GCNA proteins is generally conserved, although in some species one or more domains have been lost through modular protein evolution.
source: This four-domain architecture is generally conserved in GCNA proteins, although in some species, including mouse, one or more domains have been lost through modular protein evolution, bringing remarkable variation to the GCNA family (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplements 2 and 3) (Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: Comparative domain architecture analysis across GCNA orthologs.

claim: S. pombe GCNA does not have an IDR, but a related fission yeast, S. japonicus, does.
source: Of note, S. pombe does not have an IDR, but a related fission yeast, S. japonicus, does (not shown).
evidence: Disorder prediction analysis of fission yeast GCNA proteins.

claim: In animals that generate germ cells from adult multipotent cells, Gcna is expressed in both the multipotent stem cells and the germ cells derived from them.
source: In animals that generate germ cells from adult multipotent cells, Gcna is expressed more broadly in two cell types that have gametogenic potential and thus carry the heritable genome – the multipotent stem cells and the germ cells derived from them.
evidence: Expression data from organisms with multipotent stem cells that give rise to germ cells.

claim: In Hydra, germ cells are derived from interstitial stem cells.
source: In the cnidarian Hydra, germ cells are derived from interstitial stem cells, where Gcna expression is upregulated compared with two exclusively somatic stem cell lineages (Littlefield, 1985; Bosch et al., 2010; Hemmrich et al., 2012).
evidence: Published studies of Hydra stem cell biology.

claim: In planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea and the acoel Hofstenia miamia, neoblasts are totipotent adult stem cell populations from which germ cells arise.
source: In the planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea, and the acoel Hofstenia miamia, Gcna is upregulated in neoblasts, the totipotent adult stem cell populations from which germ cells arise (van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014; Srivastava et al., 2014).
evidence: Published studies of planarian and acoel stem cell biology.

claim: Gcna is enriched in the germlines of animals that segregate their germlines in the first cell division of the embryo due to maternally inherited factors, including C. elegans, Drosophila, zebrafish, and frog.
source: Gcna is enriched in the germlines of animals such as C. elegans, Drosophila, zebrafish, and frog, which segregate their germlines in the first cell division of the embryo due to maternally inherited factors (Figure 5B,C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—source data 2) (Tomancak et al., 2002; Graveley et al., 2011; Reinke et al., 2004; Robinson et al., 2013; Kohara and Shin-i, 1998).
evidence: Published expression data from multiple organisms with preformed germline.

claim: Mouse specifies germ cells later in the embryo through inductive signals.
source: Likewise, mouse, which specifies germ cells later in the embryo through inductive signals, shows a 13-fold upregulation of Gcna transcript in the testis compared to somatic tissues (Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: Published knowledge of mouse germ cell specification.

claim: Gcna expression was present and likely enriched in cells carrying a heritable genome in the last common ancestor of all extant eukaryotes.
source: Gcna expression across all of these modalities indicates that Gcna was present, and was likely enriched in cells carrying a heritable genome, in the last common ancestor of all extant eukaryotes.
evidence: Inference based on widespread expression pattern in reproductive cells across eukaryotic diversity.

claim: Two independent mutant alleles of C. elegans gcna-1 were created using CRISPR.
source: We decided to further investigate gcna-1 function in C. elegans by creating two independent mutant alleles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of mutant generation methods and allele characterization.

claim: The ne4334 allele of C. elegans gcna-1 is a 2-bp deletion resulting in a stop codon after seven amino acids.
source: The nature of the alleles (on LGIII) is as follows: ne4334: 6007556/6007557–6007558/6007559 (2-bp deletion, stop codon after seven amino acids)
evidence: Sequencing data characterizing the mutant allele.

claim: The ne4356 allele of C. elegans gcna-1 is a 1748-bp deletion that removes the ATG start codon.
evidence: Sequencing and PCR data characterizing the mutant allele.

claim: A conditional allele of Gcna was created in mouse with Exon 4 flanked by LoxP sites.
source: Targeting vector was designed and built as in the KOMP (RRID:SCR_007318) pipeline (Skarnes et al., 2011) to ultimately generate an allele with Exon 4 of mouse Gcna flanked by LoxP sites.
evidence: Description of gene targeting strategy.

claim: Mice were bred to Ddx4/Mouse vasa homolog cre mice to delete exon 4 in vivo.
source: Mice were bred to Ddx4/Mouse vasa homolog cre mice (MvhCre-mOrange) (Hu et al., 2013) to delete exon 4 in vivo.
evidence: Description of breeding strategy to generate germline-specific deletion.

claim: The last common ancestor of C. elegans and mouse lived about 600 million years ago.
source: We provide evidence that GCNA functions in reproduction in two organisms – C. elegans and mouse – whose last common ancestor lived about 600 million years ago (Cartwright and Collins, 2007; Parfrey et al., 2011; Peterson et al., 2008)
evidence: Published phylogenetic analyses and divergence time estimates.

claim: The GCNA protein features an intrinsically disordered region with an unusual and rapidly evolving amino acid sequence that has kept this protein hidden from researchers.
source: The GCNA protein features, and in mice consists entirely of, an intrinsicially disordered region with an unusual and rapidly evolving amino acid sequence that has kept this protein hidden from researchers until now.
evidence: Inference based on lack of prior identification despite widespread antibody use.

claim: Alignment-based searches using the amino acid sequence of mouse GCNA as bait failed to detect significant similarity to any protein in any species.
source: Alignment-based searches using the amino acid sequence of mouse GCNA as bait failed to detect significant similarity to any protein in any species, suggesting that GCNA might be unique to mice.
evidence: Results of BLAST and alignment-based homology searches.

claim: GCNA could be rapidly evolving, as is common for disordered proteins due to their low level of structural constraint.
source: Alternatively, GCNA could be rapidly evolving, as is common for disordered proteins due to their low level of structural constraint (Brown et al., 2010; Huntley and Golding, 2000; Tompa, 2003).
evidence: Published studies of disordered protein evolution.

claim: A combination of methods that accommodate rapid evolution were used to identify GCNA orthologs in a broad swath of organisms from human to the most primitive single-celled eukaryotes.
source: Using a combination of methods that accommodate rapid evolution, we were able to identify GCNA orthologs in a broad swath of organisms from human to the most primitive single-celled eukaryotes.
evidence: Description of ortholog identification strategy using synteny and HMMs.

claim: GCNA orthologs were identified in human and other vertebrates by synteny.
source: Therefore, starting with mouse GCNA, which is encoded by a gene on the X chromosome, we identified orthologs in human and other vertebrates by synteny (Figure 3).
evidence: Synteny analysis showing conserved genomic context.

claim: Statistical profiles (hidden Markov models or HMMs) of the sequence of each conserved region were created to identify distant GCNA orthologs.
source: We created statistical profiles (hidden Markov models or HMMs) of the sequence of each conserved region (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of HMM construction and use for ortholog identification.

claim: Each conserved region in GCNA has a unique signature found only in GCNA orthologs, allowing unambiguous identification of orthologs in a diverse array of eukaryotic species.
source: We found that each region has a unique signature found only in GCNA orthologs, allowing us to unambiguously identify such orthologs in a diverse array of eukaryotic species, more than two hundred in all (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: HMM search results identifying over 200 GCNA orthologs.

claim: GCNA orthologs almost invariably have a large non-alignable IDR at their N-terminus despite being discovered using alignable structured domains.
source: Interestingly, even though we discovered GCNA orthologs using alignable structured domains, our amino acid charge/hydropathy analysis reveals that, almost invariably, the proteins have a large non-alignable IDR at their N-terminus (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Charge-hydropathy analysis of identified GCNA orthologs.

claim: Mouse and human GCNA proteins share highly repetitive and acidic IDRs despite not being readily aligned using conventional approaches.
source: Indeed, a comparison of mouse and human GCNA proteins showed that, while they were not readily aligned using conventional approaches, they do share highly repetitive and acidic IDRs (Figure 1D) (Nolte et al., 2001).
evidence: Comparison of IDR properties between mouse and human GCNA.

claim: The GCNA1 antibody was generated from rats immunized with cell lysates from adult mouse testis.
source: The GCNA1 and TRA98 monoclonal antibodies, generated independently from rats immunized with cell lysates from adult mouse testis, are robust markers of mouse germ cell nuclei and show no reactivity to somatic cells (Enders and May, 1994; Tanaka et al., 2000).
evidence: Published description of antibody generation.

claim: The TRA98 antibody was generated independently from rats immunized with cell lysates from adult mouse testis.
source: The GCNA1 and TRA98 monoclonal antibodies, generated independently from rats immunized with cell lysates from adult mouse testis, are robust markers of mouse germ cell nuclei and show no reactivity to somatic cells (Enders and May, 1994; Tanaka et al., 2000).
evidence: Published description of antibody generation.

claim: The developmental timing and cell type specificity of labeling with GCNA1 resembles that of TRA98.
source: The developmental timing and cell type specificity of labeling with GCNA1 resembles that of TRA98, a second antibody with an unknown antigen (Tanaka et al., 2000; Inoue et al., 2011).
evidence: Published characterization of antibody staining patterns.

claim: TRA98 has a reticular or netlike localization in the nucleus similar to GCNA1.
source: The subcellular localization of GCNA1 and TRA98 also show striking similarities; we find that GCNA forms a distinctive coating around condensed chromosomes in meiotic prophase (Figure 1C), and TRA98 has been noted to have a similar reticular or netlike localization in the nucleus (Inoue et al., 2011).
evidence: Published description of TRA98 localization and comparison to GCNA1 localization data.

claim: 26 unique peptides representing 51% coverage of GCNA were detected in the GCNA1 immunoprecipitate.
source: We detected 26 unique peptides representing 51% coverage of an unannotated protein specifically in the immunoprecipitate, enabling us to confidently identify it as GCNA (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data from GCNA1 immunoprecipitation.

claim: Immunoprecipitation using TRA98 yielded 24% coverage of the GCNA protein.
source: Indeed, immunoprecipitation using TRA98 yielded 24% coverage of the GCNA protein (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Mass spectrometry data from TRA98 immunoprecipitation.

claim: Disrupting the gene encoding GCNA in mouse embryonic stem cells resulted in depletion of antigens recognized by both GCNA1 and TRA98 antibodies.
source: Additionally, we disrupted the gene encoding GCNA in mouse embryonic stem (ES) cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and found that antigens recognized by both antibodies were depleted, confirming that GCNA1 and TRA98 antibodies recognize the same protein (Figure 1F).
evidence: Western blot of mutant ES cell lysate showing loss of both antigens.
